The Situational Awareness situation.

It is now being reported that the AI hedge fund has exited its entire public equity portfolio this month.

But, what does this really mean?

As of July 1st, the Net Asset Value (NAV) of the fund is now being reported to have been ~$45 billion.

First, let's put this into perspective.

NAV = (Assets − Liabilities). This is the fund's equity capital, also known as the investors' money after accounting for borrowings.

This is NOT the same as the size of the fund's positions, particularly because the fund has been known for utilizing extreme amounts of leverage. For example:

1. At 2x leverage, a $45 billion NAV supports ~$90 billion of gross market exposure
2. At 3x leverage, that rises to ~$135 billion
3. At 4x leverage, that rises to ~ $180 billion

This means that exiting its "public equity book" does not necessarily imply $45 billion of stock changed hands. It was likely much more.

Depending on the fund's leverage and portfolio construction, the gross amount of securities unwound could have been well in excess of $100 billion.

When considering these facts, the market has actually held up exceptionally well.

There has never been an era of investing like the AI era.

Volatility is the new normal.

The leaders are different depending on what you measure:

@RobinhoodApp wins distribution.
@Ondo wins capital.
@xStocksFi wins activity.

Tbh, I find this much healthier than one platform and one chain owning almost the entire category.

AI-driven drug discovery could substantially reduce the cost and time required to develop a drug candidate.

Rentosertib is the clearest example so far. According to Insilico Medicine, the program moved from hypothesis to a preclinical candidate in under 18 months. Rentosertib’s preclinical work came in near $2.6 million against a conventional $15-25 million. Insilico published peer-reviewed Phase IIa results in Nature Medicine.

One successful program cannot establish the economics of an entire platform. Rentosertib targeted idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, a well-characterized disease with established clinical endpoints. It's still too early to know whether this approach can deliver similar timelines and costs in more complex disease areas.

About $230B in branded U.S. drug sales are at risk of generic or biosimilar competition between 2025 and 2030. Partnerships may become a more natural route for pharmaceutical companies seeking access to AI-driven discovery without taking on the risk of building the entire stack themselves.

If other programs produce similar results, more of the value in drug discovery could move toward full-stack platforms that license their capabilities to pharma.

My thoughts on the Fed that told us nothing and how the bond market responded. 

Rates unchanged yesterday, exactly as I told you. 

That was the easy part. What came with it was nothing. No forward guidance, not one sentence about September. The statement barely moved except for the dissent list.

3 dissents. Logan, Hammack, Kashkari, all for 25 bps. FinX called it a hawkish tell. It isn’t. Warsh wants the argument in the open, where prior chairs got unanimity that was mostly theater. So 3 dissents under him means less, not more, and those 3 have been the hawkish end of the table all along.

The market moved my way. September hike odds fell to 60% from 80%. Fewer people believe a hike is coming, not more, and that number still has room to fall.

Now the part everyone should be focusing on.

The most important market yesterday was Treasuries. The 30-year rose 12.1 bps to 5.213%, highest since 2007. Real yields rose with it, so the actual cost of capital got worse. 10s2s steepened. That is a bond market pricing a Fed behind the curve, and pricing it aggressively.

The fear is not really about oil. What’s spooking the long end is AI capex. Chips and memory. Power. Copper, silver and gold all higher the same day. One commodity rising is a story about that commodity. All of them rising at once is capital being fire hosed into every physical corner of the economy.

I’ll say the thing I always say, because I believe it and because it limits how far I’ll push this. Sustained inflation is a monetary phenomenon. Oil doubling is a relative price change. But when hundreds of billions chase a fixed stock of transformers, turbines, HBM capacity and electricians on four-year lead times, the money is real and the supply is finite, and the bond market has decided that’s close enough. Whether it’s textbook correct matters less than the 30-year sitting at 5.21% and still climbing.

Which gives you the ugliest setup I’ve seen in a while, because stocks and bonds want opposite things.

Stocks want a cut, or a clear one-and-done hike so the pain has an end date. Bonds want a hike badly, because that’s the only way this Fed shows resolve on inflation. Bonds aren’t asking nicely. They’re selling until they get an answer.

The best outcome for both is the Fed telegraphing 25 bps for September. Calms the long end, doesn’t signal a cycle. I don’t think they deliver it, same as I didn’t think they’d hike.

Until they do, you’re long a tape where the bond market votes against you every day.

It is good he’s done selling, and it’s generally a smart to take the other side of liquidations as a trade. 

Now we’ve bounced quite hard .. but far below where the liquidations started. So perhaps still a trade left — but are we even capable of getting to the highs?

To answer that the major question becomes “is there enough capital that believes in the LT (Leo Thesis) to take us back to the highs even if L himself isn’t there.”

There’s an argument that a lot of managers were on the sidelines and there is substantial capital willing to allocate now, at these “better” prices, but the volatility of these names limit exposure among the people with real risk limits (which L clearly did not have)

Gut instinct says capital will flow in and we do see a rally higher quickly, after some churn here.

PEAQ remains the most interesting bet in crypto x AI on the cambrian explosion of physical AI and robotics.

I get the concern but I'd measure or phrase it a bit differently.

-It's less of an attack, imo, and more-so the existing system adopting to the latest tech to keep extending itself. And notably, people who *use* the existing system built stablecoins, not the system itself (e.g. stablecoins were built on the margins, and only when they grew large did Uncle Sam realize it could benefit them). This is inevitably going to last a long time, imo. Those that consider it an attack should buckle in.

-Taxes are a friction, which is why I support tax exemptions on modest btc spending amounts (as a realistic start) rather than the focus on crypto securities that recent legislation emphasizes. But it's not surprising that this part keeps getting dropped, and that has to be expected. They're not going to make it easy.

-People want their near-term capital to be relatively stable. And they often want what they are paid in to match their liabilities (what they owe others). Those aspects contribute to why, organically, stablecoins are quite desired globally (less-so in the US, where we have countless USD payment options).

-Stablecoins can be frozen/confiscated, unlike bitcoin. But for people who perceive themselves as low risk of being targeted that way and with small/medium amounts, millions of people simply don't run into that freezing/confiscation problem and so they enjoy those other aspects of stablecoins for working capital and payments. Those that need or want the more permissionless aspect are more likely to be early bitcoin adopters for MoE.

-Imo, the stepping stone to keep bitcoin on the SoV-MoE-UoA pathway is to make sure it's increasingly *exchangeable*. In other words, a key reason why a gold coin is valuable is because I can carry it with me globally, and pretty easily find a buyer for it almost anywhere at a decent market price. I can't easily buy goods or services with it directly (because it's not what businesses use as their working capital or what they have liabilities denominated in), but I can convert it readily to whatever the local money is in most places. That global exchange feature is something I can't do with most other SoVs like stocks. Bitcoin scores decently in that regard but needs to keep getting better. That intermediate step is a key stepping stone to further improve. Expecting massive volumes of btc last-mile payments any time soon is going to lead to disappointment, imo, even though it's important to build the infrastructure for it (and plan company burn rates for the long haul, rather than be shocked when volumes don't explode a couple years in). But expecting to be able to exchange bitcoin for liquid value in most places you go like gold without much friction is a more intermediate-term realistic expectation to keep working toward, with high-volume MoE further out.

I can't easily buy goods or services with it directly (because it's not what businesses use as their working capital or what they have liabilities denominated in), but I can convert it readily to whatever the local money is in most places. That intermediate step is a key stepping stone to further improve. Expecting massive volumes of btc last-mile payments any time soon is going to lead to disappointment, imo, even though it's important to build the infrastructure for it (and plan company burn rates for the long haul, rather than be shocked when volumes don't explode a couple years in). We spent 2 years calling Chinese AI models "cheap copycats."

Last week something changed the space forever, and almost nobody in crypto is connecting it to DeAI yet.

What happened? Kimi K3.

Moonshot released Kimi K3 for anyone to download and run.

It's the biggest open model ever released, and independent rankings put only three models on the planet ahead of it (all closed American models such as Claude and GPT).

The difference is money. Chinese open models are running 60 to 90% cheaper than Claude and GPT.

And developers have already switched. On OpenRouter (the platform devs use to access AI models), Chinese models now handle 3x more traffic than American ones.

A year ago it was the reverse.

How does this affect DeAI?

Open models are the backbone of DeAI. Training new models in a decentralized way is still too hard, so most DeAI projects today are really doing one thing: running open models and selling access to them.

So the bet looks like this:

Better open models → more demand to run them → a bigger market for DeAI to compete for.

But let's be real: better open models don't mean DeAI automatically wins. Devs can just buy access from big centralized companies instead.

K3 shifts this in DeAI's favor though.

The model is so massive that Moonshot recommends 64+ GPUs just to run it. Nobody's running this at home, which means everyone who wants K3 has to pay someone to run it for them.

That's the market.

And DeAI providers have an angle the centralized guys can't copy: private access with no signups and no KYC. @AskVenice is already offering K3 on exactly that pitch.

There's also a catch in the fine print that most people haven't read.

K3 isn't fully free to use. Any company selling access to K3 needs a separate deal with Moonshot once they make over $20m a year.

And that $20m counts everything the company makes, not just what they make from K3.

Small networks are fine today. The catch only matters once a provider gets big, and how decentralized networks handle that is an open question worth watching.

Which brings me to the two areas I'm watching. These are two different trades.

Inference layers (the platforms selling access to models):

@AskVenice (already serving K3)
@dphnAI
@chutes_ai
@OpenGradient

GPU networks (the raw computing power):

@AethirCloud
@akashnet
@ionet

One nuance on the second group: a model this big needs serious data center hardware in one place. A network stitched together from random gaming PCs around the world can't run it.

So not every GPU network benefits equally from this era.

What I'm watching to confirm or kill the thesis:

• Usage numbers on the inference platforms
• GPU demand and pricing on the compute networks
• Open model share on OpenRouter (already the majority, does it keep climbing)

The thesis isn't that DeAI wins because open models got good.

It's that the market DeAI competes for just got permanently bigger, and the networks are priced like nothing changed.

I'm probably missing some good ones. Who else is on your radar?

Inference layers (the platforms selling access to models):

@AskVenice (already serving K3)
@dphnAI
@chutes_ai
@OpenGradient

GPU networks (the raw computing power):

@AethirCloud
@akashnet
@ionet

One nuance on the second group: a model this big needs serious data center hardware in one place. A network stitched together from random gaming PCs around the world can't run it.

So not every GPU network benefits equally from this era.

What I'm watching to confirm or kill the thesis:

• Usage numbers on the inference platforms
• GPU demand and pricing on the compute networks
• Open model share on OpenRouter (already the majority, does it keep climbing)

The thesis isn't that DeAI wins because open models got good.

It's that the market DeAI competes for just got permanently bigger, and the networks are priced like nothing changed.

I'm probably missing some good ones. Who else is on your radar?

This is basically the first step of the hard takeoff scenario. So it’s not “AI suddenly wakes up and becomes a god”, but AI starts improving the system that runs and trains AI, in domains where progress is measurable and verifiable.

GPT-5.6 Sol is already analyzing production traffic, finding load-balancing inefficiencies, testing new routing strategies, rewriting GPU kernels and validating the results. Those kernel optimizations cut serving costs by 20% (so billions of $$$)

It also designed and ran hundreds of experiments to improve its own speculative decoding model, launched the training runs, monitored them, and intervened when hardware failed or training became unstable. Result: 15%+ more token-generation efficiency (which means freeing more compute and reducing cost). 

This is recursive self-improvement in its early, very practical form! The model improves the engineering stack, which makes the model cheaper and faster, which gives researchers more compute and more experiments, which produces a better model…

Today this works best in software engineering because the output is easy to measure: does the kernel compile, is it correct, is latency lower, did cost go down? Soon the same loop moves into AI research itself: experiment design, architecture search, training recipes, data generation, evals, debugging training runs.

At that point it is no longer just “AI helping engineers work faster.” It is AI accelerating the process that creates the next AI. 

That is the hard takeoff path to the singularity (AGI). Not one magical jump, but a feedback loop that keeps getting faster. If you want to be fancy you can say: « This is the beginning of a recursive self-improvement loop toward the singularity. »

I think this is massively underappreciated. LLMs still generalize surprisingly badly. A teenager can learn to drive with maybe 30 hours of practice and then handle roads and situations they have never seen before. An AI system needs an absurd amount of driving data (like trillions of hours!), simulation and edge cases to achieve the same reliability.

And this is true in basically every field. Coding, biology, finance, healthcare, office work. As long as models cannot generalize from a few examples like humans do, we will need gigantic amounts of high quality, task-specific and verifiable data just to teach them what we consider basic work.

Compute gets most of the attention, but data is just as important and it's getting more and more expensive.
